title: The Tribe of Levi: Priests, Singers, and Cities
summary: At the center of the genealogies stands Levi, the tribe set apart for God's service. The chapter traces the high priestly line from Aaron to Jehozadak, who went into exile, lists the three Levite clans, names the singers David appointed (Heman, Asaph, and Ethan) with their ancestry back to Levi, distinguishes the priests' work of atonement, and lists the towns given to the Levites throughout the land.
story: The genealogies have covered the southern tribes and those east of the Jordan. Now, at the physical center of the nine chapters, the Chronicler places Levi. That placement is deliberate: for him, the worship of God is the heart of Israel's life, and the tribe that served at God's house stands in the middle of the people. The chapter is long and dense, but it tells the reader what the rest of 1 Chronicles will care about. David will bring the ark to Jerusalem and appoint singers; Solomon will build the temple and the priests will serve there. Here, before any of that is narrated, the Chronicler shows that the people who will carry out that worship have a lineage reaching back to Levi and Aaron, and that their service continued through the exile to his own day.
historical:
In the Hebrew Bible this chapter is numbered 5:27 to 6:66, so English and Hebrew verse numbers differ by fifteen verses; the words are the same. The high priestly list in verses 1 to 15 runs from Aaron, brother of Moses, to Jehozadak, who went into exile when Nebuchadnezzar took Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC. Several names can be matched with events: Zadok served under David and Solomon (2 Samuel 8:17; 1 Kings 2:35), Hilkiah found the book of the law in the temple in the reign of Josiah around 622 BC (2 Kings 22), and Seraiah was executed by the Babylonians at Riblah after the city fell (2 Kings 25:18-21). Jehozadak's son Joshua (or Jeshua) became high priest after the return (Haggai 1:1; Ezra 3:2), which makes this list the priestly bridge from the first temple to the second.

The list is selective. It follows only the line of Eleazar and Zadok and passes over high priests known from Kings, such as Jehoiada in the days of Joash, as well as the house of Eli from Ithamar's line. The list of Levitical towns in verses 54 to 81 closely parallels Joshua 21, which describes the allotment of forty-eight towns with their pasturelands to the Levites, as Numbers 35:1-8 had commanded.
cultural:
The Levites had no tribal territory of their own. Numbers 18:20-24 explains that the LORD himself was their inheritance, and they lived from the tithes and offerings of the people. Instead of a region, they received towns scattered through all the tribes, with the pasture land around them for their animals. This spread God's servants throughout Israel. Some of these towns were also cities of refuge, places where a person who had killed someone accidentally could flee and be protected from revenge until a proper judgment (Numbers 35; Joshua 20). Hebron and Shechem are named here as such cities.

The chapter carefully distinguishes the work of the priests from that of the other Levites. Only Aaron's descendants offered sacrifices on the altar, burned incense, and served in the Most Holy Place to make atonement (verse 49). The other Levites did every kind of service of the tabernacle (verse 48): carrying, guarding, maintaining, and, from David's time on, singing and playing music. Singing in worship was not a casual addition but an office, with families appointed to it and trained for it, as chapter 25 will show in detail.
literary: The chapter is built from several lists placed side by side. There are two lists of Levi's sons (verses 1 to 3 and 16 to 19), which introduce two kinds of genealogy: the high priestly line (verses 4 to 15) and the three Levite clans (verses 20 to 30). The genealogies of the singers (verses 33 to 47) run in the opposite direction, from the singer back to Levi, as if climbing the family tree. Heman stands in the center, with Asaph on his right and Ethan on his left, the arrangement of a choir. Verses 49 to 53 return to Aaron's line, and the list of towns closes the chapter. The repetition is not careless. It shows the whole tribe from different angles: by descent, by office, and by place.

outline.t: The high priestly line from Levi to the exile
The clans of Gershom, Kohath, and Merari
The singers David appointed and their ancestry
The priests' work of atonement and Aaron's line
The towns and pasturelands of the Levites

doctrines.note: Verse 49 names the heart of the priests' work: to make atonement for Israel through the offerings on the altar, as Moses commanded. Israel's life with a holy God depended on sacrifice offered by those he appointed.
The careful distinction between priests and Levites, and the attention to who may serve in the Most Holy Place, reflects God's holiness. Approaching him was a privilege given, not a right claimed.

The Levites were scattered in towns throughout every tribe, and the singers led God's people in praise. The chapter pictures worship as the shared life of the whole people, served by those set apart for it.

words.note: Kipper, to make atonement (verse 49). It means to cover, cleanse, or ransom, removing the guilt and impurity that separate a people from God so that he can dwell among them. In the Old Testament atonement is God's provision, carried out through appointed sacrifices, not a human attempt to buy his favor.

Shir, song. David put these Levites in charge of song in the house of the LORD (verse 31). Chronicles gives music a dignity that other historical books don't, treating it as part of the ordered worship of God.

Migrash, pastureland, the open ground around a town used for grazing. The word occurs over forty times in the chapter's list of Levitical towns. It reminds the reader that the Levites, though set apart for worship, also lived ordinary lives with flocks and herds.

Avodah, service or work. The same word can mean labor and worship. The Levites' service (verses 32 and 48) covered everything from carrying the tabernacle to leading songs, all of it counted as service to God.

christ: The chapter's priestly line runs from Aaron to the exile and on to the second temple, but its central point is verse 49: priests made atonement for Israel by the sacrifices God commanded. The letter to the Hebrews reads this whole system as a pattern pointing forward. It says that Jesus is a high priest not from Levi but from Judah, in the order of Melchizedek (Hebrews 7:11-17), and that he offered himself once for all rather than repeating sacrifices daily (Hebrews 7:27; 9:11-12). The Levitical priesthood was real, given by God, and truly served Israel; the New Testament presents it as preparing for the one priest whose sacrifice needs no successor. The chapter's singers also anticipate the New Testament's picture of God's people as a community of praise (Colossians 3:16).

hard.q: Was Samuel a Levite or an Ephraimite?
hard.a: In verses 27 and 28 and again in verses 33 to 38, Samuel appears in the Levitical clan of Kohath, and his grandson Heman is a leading singer. Yet 1 Samuel 1:1 introduces his father Elkanah as a man from the hill country of Ephraim, and some translations call him an Ephraimite. Interpreters answer this in several ways. Many argue that 1 Samuel describes where Elkanah lived rather than his tribe: Levites lived in towns throughout the other tribes, including Ephraim (verse 66 lists Ephraimite towns given to the Kohathites), so a Levite could be called an Ephraimite by residence. Others think Samuel's family was adopted into the Levites because of his priestly service, or that the Chronicler is expressing Samuel's role in Levitical terms. The first explanation fits the chapter's own information about Levitical towns, and it has many defenders. Whatever the explanation, Samuel's service at the tabernacle, which included offering sacrifices, fits the Chronicler's picture of him within the tribe that served God's house.

questions: The Levites had no land of their own because God was their inheritance. What would it mean for you to treat God himself as your portion rather than what he gives?
The Chronicler treats singing in worship as a real office with appointed people. How seriously do you take the songs you sing to God?
The chapter distinguishes different kinds of service, all of them needed. What service are you called to among God's people, and how does it connect to the work of others?
